limitations: Small effect size and lack of interaction effect when modeling 3-back and 2-back working memory tasks together.
Testing was not conducted under ideal experimental conditions, with post-environment testing on cell phones in distracting lobby/entry ways.
Potential for reduced cognitive improvement due to frequent survey pings on mobile devices during walks.
Inability to replicate previous findings on trait impulsivity and positive affect in natural environments, possibly due to different study design (experimental vs. observational).
Limited statistical power for observing relationships for individual differences due to between-subject analyses.
Uncertainty regarding the duration of observed differences in affect and thought content after leaving each environment.
Possible attenuation of some differences by the end of the hour-long walk due to participants fully exploring the spaces.
Technical difficulties prevented participants from taking pictures during surveys to link visual features with thought content.
Generalizability limitations due to participants visiting locations without companions.
Study limited to one natural (conservatory) and one commercial (mall) space in a single North American city.
Differences between locations extend beyond naturalness (e.g., demographics of other visitors, purpose of visits), which may influence results.
Cultural differences in public space purposes and comfort may influence results.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the immediate impacts of natural (conservatory) versus commercial (mall) semi-public indoor spaces on affect, thought content, and working memory. Using repeated surveys during a one-hour walk, participants in the conservatory reported more past-oriented, positive, and exciting thoughts, higher positive affect, increased creativity, and a greater sense of 'getting away' from concerns, alongside reduced impulsivity. Conversely, the mall environment was associated with more future-oriented thoughts and higher impulsive buying. Working memory performance (2-back) also showed greater improvement after the conservatory walk. Individual differences in traits like intellect and reflection moderated some of these effects. Limitations include potential distractions during testing, limited generalizability from a single city's locations, and the inability to fully explore the time course of all effects.
